questions.question: Which pair best describes encapsulation in Java?
options: Private fields and methods that control access to them
Many methods with the same name
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides the data with private and lets other code change it only through the class's own methods.

questions.question: What is a class invariant?
options: A local variable that never changes
A rule that must stay true for every object, such as a count never being negative
A constant declared in an interface
questions.explanation: An invariant is a condition the class promises after every public call. Private fields let one class keep that promise.

questions.question: class Pass { private int visits; void set(int v) { if (v >= 0) visits = v; } int get() { return visits; } } Pass p = new Pass(); p.set(8); p.set(-3); System.out.println(p.get()); What is printed?
questions.explanation: The setter ignores -3 because it fails the check, so the field keeps its earlier value 8.

questions.question: class Plan { private final List<String> c; Plan(List<String> c) { this.c = c; } List<String> get() { return c; } } List<String> x = new ArrayList<>(); Plan p = new Plan(x); x.add("Yoga"); System.out.println(p.get()); What is printed?
questions.explanation: The constructor stored the caller's list itself, not a copy, so the later add shows up inside Plan.

questions.question: A class has private final List<String> items and public List<String> getItems() { return items; }. What is the flaw?
options: Callers can add or remove items through the returned list
questions.explanation: final stops the field from pointing to another list, but the list itself is still mutable. Return a copy or a read-only view.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT needed to make a class immutable?
options: Provide a public setter for each field
Copy mutable arguments in the constructor
questions.explanation: Setters change state, so an immutable class has none. The other three are standard steps.

questions.question: A setter checks that age is between 1 and 99, but the constructor does this.age = age; directly. What can go wrong?
options: An object can be created with an invalid age like -4
questions.explanation: Validation must also run in the constructor, for example by calling the setter, or invalid objects can be created.

questions.question: final class Card { private final String plan; Card(String p) { plan = p; } Card with(String p) { return new Card(p); } String plan() { return plan; } } Card a = new Card("Basic"); Card b = a.with("Gold"); System.out.println(a.plan() + " " + b.plan()); What is printed?
questions.explanation: with returns a new Card and leaves a unchanged, which is how immutable classes model a change.

questions.question: How does encapsulation differ from abstraction?
options: They are two names for the same idea
Encapsulation protects an object's data; abstraction hides how a task is done
Encapsulation needs interfaces; abstraction needs private fields
Abstraction only applies to static methods
questions.explanation: Encapsulation asks who may touch the data. Abstraction asks what a type can do, without showing how.

questions.question: What does Collections.unmodifiableList(list) return?
options: A deep copy that can be edited freely
A read-only view that throws on add or remove
A sorted copy of the list
questions.explanation: It wraps the list in a view whose change methods throw UnsupportedOperationException, so callers can only read.
